column4: The section treats the camel as familiar wealth and a source of everyday provision before the final return to God. This ayah says pregnant she-camels are abandoned amid the Last-Day upheaval; a normally valuable herd is neglected when judgment arrives.

The section's lexical note for the root ر ف ع calls a she-camel that holds colostrum in her udder a rāfiʿ, while 88:13 has raised couches. This ayah repeats the raised-couch garden scene, making the root's shift from bodily holding to elevated furnishings concrete.

The section develops مَصْفُوفَة as rows of cushions and, in its lexical note, rows of sacrificial camels. This ayah describes the blessed reclining on couches مَصْفُوفَة, carrying the same ordered furnishing into the garden scene.

The section names the root س ع ي for the striving of the garden's satisfied faces. This ayah says a person has only what they strove for, making the link between earthly effort and the section's contentment in the afterlife explicit.
The section names سَعْي as effort and says the garden's faces are satisfied with it. This ayah says that effort will be seen, adding the disclosure of the work whose outcome the section describes.
The section's faces are pleased with their striving. This continuation says each person will then be repaid with the fullest recompense, supplying the outcome of the striving named in 53:39–40.

The section places the camel beneath a sky described as raised. This neighboring creation passage says the sky's ceiling was raised and proportioned, echoing the sky that frames the camel in 88:17–20.

The section's creation gaze ends with the spread earth around the camel. This ayah says the earth was spread out, echoing that ground in the same sequence that continues with water, pasture, and mountains.

The section describes a garden furnished with raised couches and arranged cushions. This ayah pictures the blessed reclining on couches whose linings are brocade, a specific continuation of the garden's furnishings.

The section's root note for نَاصِبَة describes a group's day-long walk, beside the exhausted labor of 88:3. This ayah says no fatigue or weariness touches the people in the enduring home, reversing toil with settled ease.

The section's root note for نَاصِبَة includes a group's whole-day walk. In this ayah Moses' companion says the journey has caused fatigue, a concrete travel use of the same root named for the section's laboring faces.

The section develops lined-up sacrificial camels and cushions, using the root ص ف ف for an ordered row. This ayah swears by those ranged in rows; whatever the rowed beings are, it gives a parallel of deliberate alignment.

The section names س م ن as the root behind ghee from milk and notes that 88:7's food does not fatten. This ayah's dream of seven fat cows consumed by seven lean cows makes animal fatness a measure of abundant and failing provision.

The section's dictionary note for خ ش ع describes a camel's hump losing fat and drooping. This ayah calls the dry earth خَاشِعَة, then says rain makes it stir and grow; the root's lowered state turns toward the fresh growth that sustains grazing animals.

The section cites camels lined for sacrifice at the pilgrimage. This ayah names the sacrificial offerings and garlands among the signs by which the Sacred House stands for people, placing the camel offering within the Hajj's public order.

The section describes people in Hell with no food except a plant that neither fattens nor relieves hunger. This ayah likewise says there is no food for the condemned but ghislin, a direct parallel in the deprivation of the afterlife meal.
